text:
Six more, quickly. Offline features are computed in batch jobs over history, and are as fresh as the last run. Online features are computed at request time, looked up in the online store or built from the request itself, like how recent the session is. Keeping the two definitions identical is the hard part. Data validation checks each new batch for schema, ranges, distributions and completeness before training. Without it, a new null column or a sensor that changes units trains a model on corrupt data, and it quietly underperforms. GPUs win on large, parallel work: batched neural networks, transformers, images and video. For a light model, like a tree ensemble scoring one request, a CPU is faster, because the GPU's launch overhead would dominate. Knowledge distillation trains a small student to match a large teacher's probabilities, not just the labels. Shown one held-out nine, our digit network says sixty-five percent nine, thirty-five percent three. That tells a student nines can look like threes; the hard label says only nine. To cut serving latency, find where the time goes, then pull these levers: a compressed model, batching under load, a cache for repeated inputs, a faster runtime or hardware, the model placed beside its callers, and a simpler model on the paths that can't wait. And under variable load, autoscale replicas on utilization or queue depth. New replicas take time to warm up, so a request queue in front lets a spike wait instead of being dropped.

Features in, predictions out, labels back: that's the system around the model. Once it's live, the world it learned from keeps changing. Next: shipping and monitoring models.
